base_method_text.title: Accelerating Convergence of Score-Based Diffusion Models, Provably
base_method_text.summary:
Score-based diffusion models, while achieving remarkable empirical
performance, often suffer from low sampling speed, due to extensive function
evaluations needed during the sampling phase. Despite a flurry of recent
activities towards speeding up diffusion generative modeling in practice,
theoretical underpinnings for acceleration techniques remain severely limited.
In this paper, we design novel training-free algorithms to accelerate popular
deterministic (i.e., DDIM) and stochastic (i.e., DDPM) samplers. Our
accelerated deterministic sampler converges at a rate $O(1/{T}^2)$ with $T$ the
number of steps, improving upon the $O(1/T)$ rate for the DDIM sampler; and our
accelerated stochastic sampler converges at a rate $O(1/T)$, outperforming the
rate $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the DDPM sampler. The design of our algorithms
leverages insights from higher-order approximation, and shares similar
intuitions as popular high-order ODE solvers like the DPM-Solver-2. Our theory
accommodates $\ell_2$-accurate score estimates, and does not require
log-concavity or smoothness on the target distribution.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces novel training-free algorithms to accelerate both deterministic (DDIM) and stochastic (DDPM) score-based diffusion models, achieving improved convergence rates of O(1/T^2) and O(1/T) respectively, without requiring stringent assumptions on the target data distribution.
base_method_text.methodology: The approach leverages insights from higher-order approximation and momentum terms to adjust the update rule in discrete time. For the deterministic sampler, it shares similar intuitions with high-order ODE solvers like DPM-Solver-2. The stochastic sampler is designed based on higher-order expansions of the conditional density.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The proposed deterministic samplers were evaluated using pre-trained score functions from Huggingface on the CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, and LSUN-Churches datasets. The image quality was visually compared for different numbers of function evaluations (NFEs).
base_method_text.limitations: The convergence theory might be sub-optimal in terms of its dependency on the problem dimension. The deterministic sampler requires stronger assumptions on the score estimates.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include refining the dimension dependency in the convergence theory, extending the algorithm and theory using ideas from third-order or higher-order ODEs, and designing higher-order solvers for SDE-based samplers.

add_method_texts.title: InstructVideo: Instructing Video Diffusion Models with Human Feedback
add_method_texts.summary:
Diffusion models have emerged as the de facto paradigm for video generation.
However, their reliance on web-scale data of varied quality often yields
results that are visually unappealing and misaligned with the textual prompts.
To tackle this problem, we propose InstructVideo to instruct text-to-video
diffusion models with human feedback by reward fine-tuning. InstructVideo has
two key ingredients: 1) To ameliorate the cost of reward fine-tuning induced by
generating through the full DDIM sampling chain, we recast reward fine-tuning
as editing. By leveraging the diffusion process to corrupt a sampled video,
InstructVideo requires only partial inference of the DDIM sampling chain,
reducing fine-tuning cost while improving fine-tuning efficiency. 2) To
mitigate the absence of a dedicated video reward model for human preferences,
we repurpose established image reward models, e.g., HPSv2. To this end, we
propose Segmental Video Reward, a mechanism to provide reward signals based on
segmental sparse sampling, and Temporally Attenuated Reward, a method that
mitigates temporal modeling degradation during fine-tuning. Extensive
experiments, both qualitative and quantitative, validate the practicality and
efficacy of using image reward models in InstructVideo, significantly enhancing
the visual quality of generated videos without compromising generalization
capabilities. Code and models will be made publicly available.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces InstructVideo, a novel approach to enhance text-to-video diffusion models using human feedback. It addresses the issue of visually unappealing and misaligned video generation by fine-tuning the models with reward signals derived from image reward models. The key contributions include reformulating reward fine-tuning as an editing process for efficiency, and using Segmental Video Reward (SegVR) and Temporally Attenuated Reward (TAR) to adapt image reward models for video.
add_method_texts.methodology: InstructVideo recasts reward fine-tuning as an editing procedure, using partial inference of the DDIM sampling chain to reduce computational costs. It employs Segmental Video Reward (SegVR) to sparsely sample frames for reward signals and Temporally Attenuated Reward (TAR) to weigh central frames more heavily, mitigating temporal modeling collapse. LoRA is used for efficient fine-tuning.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The experiments were conducted using the ModelScopeT2V model trained on the WebVid10M dataset. The prompts describing 45 animal species. HPSv2 was used as the primary reward model. Evaluation metrics included HPSv2 score and user studies to assess video quality and text alignment. Generalization was tested on new animal prompts and non-animal prompts.
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper mentions the risk of over-optimization during reward fine-tuning, which can degrade video quality despite increasing reward scores. It also acknowledges that specialized video reward models might outperform the repurposed image reward models. Additionally, the method's reliance on image reward models might not fully capture the nuances of video quality and temporal coherence.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include developing more advanced video reward models that capture human preferences for video as a whole and designing strategic mechanisms to identify and ameliorate over-optimization during reward fine-tuning. Also, it is expected to explore the adaptation to other reward functions.

base_experimental_code: The paper does not include a specific code implementation of the proposed algorithms. It refers to implementations of pre-trained score functions available in Hugging Face's Diffusers library.
base_experimental_info: The experimental setup involves using pre-trained score functions from Huggingface on datasets like CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, and LSUN-Churches for visual comparisons of image quality at different NFEs. No specific training details or metrics are provided in the context.
new_method:
Below is an example of a genuinely new method (Step 3) that draws on ideas from both the Base Method’s higher-order/accelerated diffusion sampling and the Add Method’s reward-based partial-inference approach. It aims to mitigate one of the Base Method’s core issues—namely, its lack of adaptiveness to user or external feedback during accelerated sampling—while preserving its faster convergence.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Novel Method: “Reward-Guided Accelerated Editing (ReGAE)”
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) High-Level Idea
ReGAE combines the Base Method’s accelerated sampling scheme (inspired by higher-order ODE solvers) with a reward-guided partial-inference loop (inspired by the Add Method’s idea of “recasting reward fine-tuning as editing”). Rather than running a full forward-and-reverse diffusion cycle every time user alignment (or any external reward signal) is desired, ReGAE intermittently “corrupts” and re-corrects the sample with guidance from a reward model, leveraging only a partial chain of steps. This preserves much of the Base Method’s reduced sampling overhead while enabling alignment in real-time.

2) Key Components
• Accelerated Diffusion Updates:
  – As in the Base Method, ReGAE uses higher-order expansions (akin to DPM-Solver-2) to achieve faster convergence (O(1/T²) for deterministic sampling, O(1/T) for stochastic).  
  – A momentum-like term carries forward estimate improvements to minimize the total number of function evaluations.

• Partial-Inference Editing:
  – Inspired by the Add Method’s approach of “recasting reward fine-tuning as editing,” ReGAE periodically intercepts the sampling trajectory.  
  – Instead of running the entire reverse diffusion from scratch, it “corrupts” the current sample slightly and then continues the next few steps, thereby integrating the feedback only through a short diffusion segment.

• Reward-Guided Alignment:
  – A reward model (trained or adapted from an image/video preference model) computes alignment scores (for instance, aesthetic quality or text prompt relevance).  
  – When the reward dips below a threshold, ReGAE triggers the partial-inference editing loop to correct the sample’s trajectory, thereby nudging it toward higher reward without restarting the entire sampling process.

3) Workflow Outline
a) Initialize sampling with the Base Method’s accelerated sampler.  
b) After every N steps (where N is chosen to balance overhead and feedback responsiveness), compute the reward score on the current sample.  
c) If the reward is above a threshold, continue with the next accelerated steps as originally planned.  
d) If the reward is below the threshold, partially corrupt the sample by adding noise (similar to an editing step), then run M accelerated steps (M < N) guided by the reward model’s gradient signal until the reward recovers.  
e) Continue until the final sample is generated or the target number of steps is reached.

4) Why This Method Is New
• It does more than just “tweak” the Base Method’s update rule. Instead, it fundamentally integrates a feedback-driven partial-inference loop within a high-order accelerated sampler.  
• The Base Method’s improvements to convergence speed remain in place, but now the generation can also be steered on-the-fly by an external reward signal, addressing alignment issues or user preferences.  
• Unlike the Add Method, which focuses on reward fine-tuning for large-scale text-to-video, ReGAE repurposes the partial-inference editing mechanism specifically to maintain accelerated sampling rates (rather than standard DDIM) and to allow dynamic mid-sampling corrections.

5) Potential Benefits
• Maintains faster convergence promised by the Base Method (fewer total sampling steps).  
• Improves adaptability by incorporating real-time or offline reward signals without having to do a full forward-backward diffusion loop each time.  
• Allows fine-grained control to steer sample generation toward desired properties or prompts while preserving the speed gains.

Overall, this new architecture—Reward-Guided Accelerated Editing—tackles the Base Method’s lack of alignment or feedback integration by weaving in partial-inference reward updates, all while upholding its accelerated convergence guarantees.
verification_policy:
Below is a concise experimental plan describing up to three realistic, Python-implementable experiments that can help demonstrate the superiority of the ReGAE method:

──────────────────────────────
1. Convergence Speed and Sample Quality Comparison

• Aim: Show that ReGAE’s accelerated sampling retains or improves upon the convergence speed and final sample quality relative to the Base Method.
• Implementation:
  - Code both the Base Method (with a higher-order solver for accelerated diffusion updates) and ReGAE.
  - Create a synthetic task (for example, sampling from a 2D Gaussian mixture or image generation with a simplified diffusion model) where convergence speed and sample quality can be quantitatively assessed.
  - Log the number of sampling steps, computation time, and a quality metric (e.g., mean squared error against a reference or a simplified “aesthetic” score computed by a reward function).
• Outcome: Demonstrate that while both methods converge quickly, ReGAE’s interleaved reward-guided editing obtains comparable or improved sample quality, especially in cases where a reward metric nudges the generation toward a desired output.

──────────────────────────────
2. Reward Intervention Effectiveness

• Aim: Validate how well the reward-guided partial-inference mechanism can steer the process in real time without the overhead of a full diffusion cycle.
• Implementation:
  - Implement a reward model (or even a proxy function) in Python that assigns high scores when the sample meets a particular property (for instance, proximity to a predefined “target region” in a 2D state space).
  - Run experiments on a test case where the base trajectory deviates from the target. At fixed intervals (every N steps), evaluate the reward.
  - When the reward falls below a set threshold, trigger a short partial-inference correction (by “corrupting” and then updating the sample over M steps).
  - Log the reward trajectory over time and compare scenarios with and without the partial-inference loop.
• Outcome: Expect to see that the ReGAE method recovers the high reward regions more rapidly than using the accelerated sampler alone, hence showing superior adaptability to feedback.

──────────────────────────────
3. Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

• Aim: Investigate how different hyperparameters affect the balance between acceleration and reward alignment.
• Key Parameters to Test:
  - N (interval between reward evaluations)
  - M (number of accelerated steps in the partial-inference editing loop)
  - The noise “corruption” amplitude prior to correction.
• Implementation:
  - Set up a grid or randomized search over these hyperparameters in Python (e.g., using libraries such as numpy or optuna for simple parameter sweeps).
  - For each combination, run the ReGAE sampling on a test problem and record both the computational cost (total steps/time) and the final reward.
  - Plot the trade-offs to identify the optimal regime where the fastest convergence is achieved without sacrificing reward alignment.
• Outcome: Provide clear evidence that suitable hyperparameter choices lead to a superior balance—maintaining the fast convergence of the Base Method while benefiting from the real-time feedback enabled by the reward-guided corrections.

──────────────────────────────
Why These Experiments?

• They are realistic to code in Python using standard scientific libraries (numpy, matplotlib, and even simple integration schemes or ODE solvers from scipy).
• They cover both aspects of the new method: rapid convergence and responsiveness to external reward signals.
• The synthetically designed tasks (e.g., 2D state sampling or image-like tasks with surrogate reward functions) allow for measurable and reproducible comparisons.

By running these experiments, one could convincingly demonstrate that the ReGAE method not only speeds up convergence but also dynamically adapts to structure in the sampling task—thereby addressing one of the Base Method’s core limitations while preserving its efficiency.
experiment_details:
Below is one detailed proposal outlining three complementary experiments that together verify the claims made in the ReGAE method. Each experiment is described in terms of its objective, rationale, detailed implementation (assuming the use of PyTorch plus supporting libraries like NumPy, matplotlib, and SciPy), and sample code snippets. The experiments are designed to be realistic, reproducible, and to require minimal reimplementation by using standard libraries and simulated tasks. They also link back to the ideas and experimental design of the original research (which used pre-trained score functions and evaluated image quality on standard datasets) but are simplified to a synthetic 2D setting for clarity and speed.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 1: Convergence Speed and Sample Quality Comparison

Objective:
• Demonstrate that ReGAE reaches high-quality samples in fewer steps or less time than a Base Method based on an accelerated sampler.
• Quantitatively compare sample quality (using a metric like mean squared error [MSE] against a target distribution) and measure convergence profiles such as iteration count and execution time.

Setup:
• Create a synthetic 2D task. For example, define a target distribution as a mixture of Gaussians in 2D.
• Implement both the Base Method and ReGAE:
  – The Base Method uses an accelerated solver (e.g., a Runge-Kutta or higher-order integration scheme) that updates samples following a diffusion process.
  – ReGAE interleaves the regular sampling steps with reward-guided corrections (partial inference) using a surrogate score function.
• Log the number of diffusion steps, wall-clock time, and a quality metric (e.g., sample MSE against the known target distribution “density map”).

Implementation details:
• Build the “diffusion update” function in PyTorch using tensor operations.
• Use the PyTorch timer utilities (or Python’s time module) to capture execution time.
• Create a function that computes the quality metric (e.g., by assigning each sample a “distance” from the target center or by comparing histograms).

Example Python Code Outline:

-----------------------------------------------------------
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import time
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Synthetic target: 2D Gaussian mixture.
def target_density(x):
    # Two centers at (-2, -2) and (2, 2)
    comp1 = torch.exp(-0.5 * torch.sum((x - torch.tensor([-2.0,-2.0]))**2, dim=1))
    comp2 = torch.exp(-0.5 * torch.sum((x - torch.tensor([2.0,2.0]))**2, dim=1))
    return comp1 + comp2

# Base diffusion update (a simplified accelerated solver)
def base_diffusion_update(x, step_size=0.1):
    noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.1
    # A simple Euler update with “accelerated” step (in practice could be higher-order)
    return x + step_size * (-x) + noise

# ReGAE update: Interleaved reward-guided correction.
def reward_guided_update(x, step_size=0.1, reward_threshold=0.8, n_partial=5):
    # Simple reward: structure is good if target_density is high
    reward = target_density(x)
    if reward.mean() < reward_threshold:
        # Trigger partial inference correction:
        for _ in range(n_partial):
            # Apply a “correction” update -- here a noise corruption followed by a mini-update driven by the score (gradient of log density)
            noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.05
            x = x + step_size * torch.autograd.grad(target_density(x).sum(), x, retain_graph=True)[0] + noise
    else:
        x = x + step_size * (-x)  # regular update
    return x

# Main experiment loop
def run_experiment(method='base', n_steps=50, n_samples=500):
    # Initialize random samples from standard normal
    x = torch.randn(n_samples, 2, requires_grad=True)
    quality_history = []
    times = []
    start_time = time.time()
    for i in range(n_steps):
        if method == 'base':
            x = base_diffusion_update(x, step_size=0.1)
        elif method == 'ReGAE':
            x = reward_guided_update(x, step_size=0.1, reward_threshold=1.0, n_partial=3)
        # Measure quality: mean squared error between target density and current density “score”
        target_scores = target_density(x).detach().numpy()
        quality = np.mean((target_scores - 1.0)**2)  # assume 1.0 is the ideal score
        quality_history.append(quality)
        times.append(time.time() - start_time)
    return x, quality_history, times

# Run and compare methods
x_base, quality_base, time_base = run_experiment(method='base')
x_regae, quality_regae, time_regae = run_experiment(method='ReGAE')

plt.plot(time_base, quality_base, label='Base Method')
plt.plot(time_regae, quality_regae, label='ReGAE')
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Quality metric (MSE)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
-----------------------------------------------------------

Expected Outcome:
• The plot should show that while both methods converge (quality metric decreases), the ReGAE method either converges faster or achieves a lower final error value while consuming similar or lower computation time.
• This experiment demonstrates that interleaving reward corrections does not degrade—and can even improve—the sample quality.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 2: Reward Intervention Effectiveness

Objective:
• Validate that the reward-guided mechanism can steer sampling trajectories in real time.
• Compare trajectories (reward over time) with and without the reward intervention.

Setup:
• Use a 2D state space with a “target region” defined (for instance, a circle centered at a given point).
• Define a reward function that gives higher rewards when the samples lie within or close to this region.
• Simulate a trajectory using the Base Method that naturally drifts away from the target.
• At fixed intervals (every N steps), check the reward and, if it falls below a threshold, trigger the partial-inference correction (ReGAE’s intervention).
• Log the reward value over steps and compare with a simulation that runs without the intervention.

Implementation details:
• Use a similar update scheme as in Experiment 1.
• Create a loop that logs the reward (computed simply based on distance from the target center).
• Compare two scenarios side by side.

Example Python Code Outline:

-----------------------------------------------------------
def reward_function(x, target_center=torch.tensor([0.0,0.0]), radius=2.0):
    # High reward if sample inside circle
    distance = torch.norm(x - target_center, dim=1)
    reward = torch.where(distance < radius, torch.tensor(1.0), torch.tensor(0.0))
    return reward

def partial_inference_edit(x, step_size=0.1, n_partial=3):
    for _ in range(n_partial):
        # Compute a pseudo grad that nudges x toward the target center
        grad = -(x - torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0]))  # simple gradient toward center
        noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.05
        x = x + step_size * grad + noise
    return x

def run_reward_experiment(n_steps=50, N=10, reward_threshold=0.5):
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=True)
    reward_history = []
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Base update step
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1
        # Evaluate reward every N steps.
        if step % N == 0:
            current_reward = reward_function(x).float().mean().item()
            reward_history.append(current_reward)
            if current_reward < reward_threshold:
                # Trigger intervention: partial inference correction.
                x = partial_inference_edit(x, step_size=0.1, n_partial=3)
        else:
            reward_history.append(reward_function(x).float().mean().item())
    return reward_history

# Run experiments with and without intervention by comparing with a simple Base Method simulation.
def run_no_intervention(n_steps=50):
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=True)
    reward_history = []
    for step in range(n_steps):
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1
        reward_history.append(reward_function(x).float().mean().item())
    return reward_history

reward_with_intervention = run_reward_experiment()
reward_without_intervention = run_no_intervention()

plt.plot(reward_with_intervention, label='ReGAE Intervention')
plt.plot(reward_without_intervention, label='Base no-intervention')
plt.xlabel("Steps")
plt.ylabel("Mean Reward")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
-----------------------------------------------------------

Expected Outcome:
• In the “with intervention” case, when the reward dips (i.e., the samples drift too far from the target region), the partial update will steer the samples back toward the target, resulting in a higher overall reward compared to the non-intervention case.
• This experiment highlights the responsiveness and effectiveness of reward-guided corrections.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

Objective:
• Analyze how key hyperparameters (reward evaluation interval N, number of partial-inference steps M, noise amplitude for corruption) affect both the convergence speed and the reward (sample quality).
• Identify the best trade-off between rapid convergence and reward alignment.

Setup:
• Extend the simulation in Experiments 1 and 2, and perform a grid search (or randomized search) over:
   – N: The interval at which reward is evaluated (e.g., 5, 10, 15 steps)
   – M: The number of partial inference correction steps (e.g., 1, 3, 5)
   – Noise amplitude for the corruption step (e.g., 0.05, 0.1, 0.2)
• For each hyperparameter combination, record the final sample quality metric (e.g., reward achieved at the end of simulation) and the total computational cost (in terms of total steps executed or wall-clock time).
• Use visualization (e.g., heat maps or line plots) to show the trade-offs.

Implementation details:
• Use Python libraries such as NumPy for grid search and matplotlib for plotting.
• Optionally, one can use Optuna or similar packages for a randomized hyperparameter search if the grid becomes large.
• Make sure to log and store results for reproducible comparisons.

Example Python Code Outline:

-----------------------------------------------------------
import itertools

def run_regae_with_params(n_steps, N, M, noise_amp):
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=True)
    rewards = []
    for step in range(n_steps):
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1  # regular base update
        if step % N == 0:
            current_reward = reward_function(x).float().mean().item()
            rewards.append(current_reward)
            if current_reward < 0.5:
                # Trigger M-step partial inference correction with adjustable noise amplitude.
                for _ in range(M):
                    grad = -(x - torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0]))
                    x = x + 0.1 * grad + torch.randn_like(x)*noise_amp
    return rewards[-1] if rewards else 0.0

# Define hyperparameter grid
Ns = [5, 10, 15]       # evaluation interval
Ms = [1, 3, 5]         # number of partial updates
noise_amps = [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]  # noise levels

results = []

for N_val, M_val, noise_val in itertools.product(Ns, Ms, noise_amps):
    final_reward = run_regae_with_params(n_steps=50, N=N_val, M=M_val, noise_amp=noise_val)
    results.append((N_val, M_val, noise_val, final_reward))
    print("N:", N_val, "M:", M_val, "Noise:", noise_val, "Final Reward:", final_reward)

# Example of plotting results in a heat map fashion (fixing one variable and varying the other two)
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(results, columns=["N", "M", "Noise", "FinalReward"])
# For instance, fix noise_amp=0.1 then pivot the table to view rewards against N and M.
df_sub = df[df["Noise"]==0.1]
pivot = df_sub.pivot(index="N", columns="M", values="FinalReward")
plt.imshow(pivot, cmap='viridis', origin='lower')
plt.colorbar(label='Final Reward')
plt.xlabel("M (Partial Steps)")
plt.ylabel("N (Reward Eval Interval)")
plt.title("Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Noise=0.1)")
plt.show()
-----------------------------------------------------------

Expected Outcome:
• The visualization should reveal clear trends. For example, there may be an optimal reward evaluation interval N and a sweet spot for the number of partial corrections M where the final reward is maximized while the computational cost is reasonable.
• This analysis will illustrate the robustness of the ReGAE method to changes in these parameters and help identify recommended default values.

──────────────────────────────
Summary

These three experiments collectively verify the two main aspects of the ReGAE method:
1. That it retains (and in some cases improves) convergence speed and quality compared to a base accelerated diffusion method.
2. That the reward-guided intervention mechanism effectively steers samples toward desired regions.
3. That there exists a range of hyperparameters for which ReGAE achieves an excellent balance between accelerated convergence and reward alignment.

By using synthetic tasks (in a 2D state space) and standard Python libraries (PyTorch, NumPy, matplotlib), the experiments maintain high reproducibility and low implementation overhead. Even though the original research used pre-trained score functions and visual datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN, etc.), these synthetic experiments simulate the core ideas and provide clear, quantitative demonstrations of the method’s advantages.

This detailed plan, along with the provided code examples, should serve as a complete experimental verification plan in line with the “Verification Policy.”
experiment_code:
Below is a complete Python script that implements all three experiments using PyTorch (with NumPy, matplotlib, Pandas, and other standard libraries). You can save this as (for example) “rega_experiments.py” and run it directly. The code prints progress messages to standard output, saves all plots in PDF format using the required filename conventions, and includes a quick self-test function that runs a minimal version of one experiment before exiting.

------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
ReGAE Experiments: Convergence Speed, Reward Intervention, and Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

Required Python libraries:
 • torch
 • numpy
 • matplotlib
 • pandas
 • itertools (standard)
 • time (standard)

Make sure to install torch, numpy, matplotlib and pandas if you have not:
  pip install torch numpy matplotlib pandas
------------------------------------------------------------
"""

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import time
import itertools
import pandas as pd

# Set random seed for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(0)
np.random.seed(0)

#############################################
# Shared functions and synthetic target definition
#############################################

def target_density(x):
    """
    Synthetic target density: a mixture of two 2D Gaussians (centers at (-2,-2) and (2,2)).
    Returns a tensor with the summed (unnormalized) density.
    """
    # Create center tensors on the same device and type as x
    center1 = x.new_tensor([-2.0, -2.0])
    center2 = x.new_tensor([2.0, 2.0])
    comp1 = torch.exp(-0.5 * torch.sum((x - center1)**2, dim=1))
    comp2 = torch.exp(-0.5 * torch.sum((x - center2)**2, dim=1))
    return comp1 + comp2

def reward_function(x, target_center=torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0])):
    """
    Simple reward function: samples inside a circle (radius=2.0) centered at target_center get reward 1.0.
    Otherwise, reward is 0.0.
    """
    # Make sure target_center is on same device and type
    target_center = x.new_tensor(target_center)
    distance = torch.norm(x - target_center, dim=1)
    reward = torch.where(distance < 2.0, torch.tensor(1.0, device=x.device), torch.tensor(0.0, device=x.device))
    return reward

#############################################
# Experiment 1: Convergence Speed and Sample Quality Comparison
#############################################

def base_diffusion_update(x, step_size=0.1):
    """
    Base method: update samples using a simple Euler diffusion update with added noise.
    """
    noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.1
    # Accelerated update (here simulated by subtracting x times step_size and adding noise)
    return x + step_size * (-x) + noise

def reward_guided_update(x, step_size=0.1, reward_threshold=0.8, n_partial=5):
    """
    ReGAE method: if the average target_density(x) is below a threshold,
    perform a partial inference correction using the gradient of the log-target.
    """
    # Enable gradient calculation since we use autograd.grad below
    x.requires_grad_(True)
    # Compute reward based on target density (the higher the density, the higher the reward)
    reward_val = target_density(x).mean().item()
    if reward_val < reward_threshold:
        print("  -> Reward below threshold; performing {} partial correction steps.".format(n_partial))
        for _ in range(n_partial):
            # Compute gradient of the summed target density with respect to x
            dens = target_density(x).sum()
            grad = torch.autograd.grad(dens, x, retain_graph=True)[0]
            noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.05
            x = x + step_size * grad + noise
            # After correction, disable the grad flag to avoid accumulating gradients from previous iteration.
            x = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    else:
        x = x + step_size * (-x)
    return x.detach()  # return tensor without gradient attached

def run_experiment(method='base', n_steps=50, n_samples=500):
    """
    Run the diffusion simulation for n_steps.
    Logs the quality metric (mean squared error against an ideal score of 1.0)
    and records the wall-clock time.
    """
    # Initialize random samples from standard normal distribution.
    # We set requires_grad=True if using the ReGAE method.
    x = torch.randn(n_samples, 2, requires_grad=True)
    quality_history = []
    times = []
    start_time = time.time()
    print("Starting experiment using method =", method)
    for i in range(n_steps):
        if method == 'base':
            x = base_diffusion_update(x, step_size=0.1)
        elif method == 'ReGAE':
            x = reward_guided_update(x, step_size=0.1, reward_threshold=1.0, n_partial=3)
        # Compute a quality metric: ideal target density score is assumed to be 1.0.
        # We use mean squared error between computed target_density(x) and 1.0.
        target_scores = target_density(x).detach().numpy()
        quality = np.mean((target_scores - 1.0)**2)
        quality_history.append(quality)
        times.append(time.time() - start_time)
        if (i+1) % 10 == 0:
            print("  Step {}: quality metric (MSE) = {:.4f}, elapsed time = {:.4f} s".format(i+1, quality, times[-1]))
    return x, quality_history, times

def experiment_1():
    print("=== Experiment 1: Convergence Speed and Sample Quality Comparison ===")
    # Run Base method
    x_base, quality_base, time_base = run_experiment(method='base', n_steps=50, n_samples=500)
    # Run ReGAE method

def partial_inference_edit(x, step_size=0.1, n_partial=3):
    """
    Partial inference correction: nudges x toward the target center (0,0) by following a simple gradient.
    """
    for _ in range(n_partial):
        # Compute a simple gradient that pushes x toward (0,0)
        grad = -(x - torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0], device=x.device))
        noise = torch.randn_like(x) * 0.05
        x = x + step_size * grad + noise
    return x

def run_reward_experiment(n_steps=50, N=10, reward_threshold=0.5):
    """
    Run simulation with reward intervention.
    Evaluate reward every N steps; if average reward is below reward_threshold,
    perform a partial inference (correction) update.
    """
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=False)
    reward_history = []
    print("Running reward intervention experiment with evaluation interval N =", N)
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Base update step (simulate drift)
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1
        # At every N steps, check reward and intervene if needed.
        if step % N == 0:
            current_reward = reward_function(x).float().mean().item()
            reward_history.append(current_reward)
            print("  Step {}: reward = {:.4f}".format(step, current_reward))
            if current_reward < reward_threshold:
                print("    -> Reward below threshold. Triggering partial inference correction.")
                x = partial_inference_edit(x, step_size=0.1, n_partial=3)
        else:
            reward_history.append(reward_function(x).float().mean().item())
    return reward_history

def run_no_intervention(n_steps=50):
    """
    Simulation without any intervention.
    """
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=False)
    reward_history = []
    print("Running base simulation with no reward intervention.")
    for step in range(n_steps):
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1
        reward_history.append(reward_function(x).float().mean().item())
    return reward_history

def experiment_2():
    print("=== Experiment 2: Reward Intervention Effectiveness ===")
    reward_with_intervention = run_reward_experiment(n_steps=50, N=10, reward_threshold=0.5)
    reward_without_intervention = run_no_intervention(n_steps=50)
    
    # Plot reward trajectories
    plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
    plt.plot(reward_with_intervention, label='ReGAE Intervention', marker='o')
    plt.plot(reward_without_intervention, label='Base No-Intervention', marker='s')

# Experiment 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis
#############################################

def run_regae_with_params(n_steps, N, M, noise_amp):
    """
    Run simulation with ReGAE-style intervention using given hyperparameters.
      N: reward evaluation interval,
      M: number of partial inference correction steps,
      noise_amp: noise amplitude during correction.
    Returns the final average reward.
    """
    x = torch.randn(500, 2, requires_grad=False)
    rewards = []
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Base update step
        x = x + 0.1 * (-x) + torch.randn_like(x)*0.1
        if step % N == 0:
            current_reward = reward_function(x).float().mean().item()
            rewards.append(current_reward)
            if current_reward < 0.5:
                # Trigger partial inference correction M times, using the adjustable noise amplitude.
                for _ in range(M):
                    grad = -(x - torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0], device=x.device))
                    x = x + 0.1 * grad + torch.randn_like(x)*noise_amp
    # If rewards list is empty (should not happen), return 0.
    return rewards[-1] if rewards else 0.0

def experiment_3():
    print("=== Experiment 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ===")
    # Define hyperparameter grid:
    Ns = [5, 10, 15]           # evaluation interval N
    Ms = [1, 3, 5]             # number of partial corrections M
    noise_amps = [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]  # noise amplitudes
    
    results = []
    
    for N_val, M_val, noise_val in itertools.product(Ns, Ms, noise_amps):
        final_reward = run_regae_with_params(n_steps=50, N=N_val, M=M_val, noise_amp=noise_val)
        results.append((N_val, M_val, noise_val, final_reward))
        print("  N:", N_val, "M:", M_val, "Noise:", noise_val, "-> Final Reward: {:.4f}".format(final_reward))
    
    # Convert the results to a Pandas DataFrame for visualization.
    df = pd.DataFrame(results, columns=["N", "M", "Noise", "FinalReward"])
    # For visualization, fix noise_amp=0.1 and pivot the table to see how N and M affect final reward.
    df_sub = df[df["Noise"]==0.1]
    pivot = df_sub.pivot(index="N", columns="M", values="FinalReward")
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.imshow(pivot, cmap='viridis', origin='lower', aspect='auto')
    plt.colorbar(label='Final Reward')
    plt.xlabel("M (Partial Steps)")
    plt.ylabel("N (Reward Eval Interval)")
    plt.title("Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Noise=0.1)")
    plt.xticks(ticks=np.arange(len(pivot.columns)), labels=pivot.columns)
    plt.yticks(ticks=np.arange(len(pivot.index)), labels=pivot.index)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("hyperparameter_sensitivity_noise0.1.pdf")
    plt.close()
    print("Experiment 3 complete. Plot saved as hyperparameter_sensitivity_noise0.1.pdf\n")
